title: XOR Games at Full Tilt: The Hardness of Binary Nonlocal Games
authors: Richard Cleve, Eric Culf, Aviv Taller
abstract: It is well known that the quantum value of an XOR nonlocal game, where the winning condition depends only on the XOR of the two players' output bits, may be approximated in polynomial time. We study a variant of the XOR game model, which we call tilted XOR games, where the winning condition can additionally depend on only one of the output bits. We show that this dramatically increases the expressive power: the computational complexity of the problem of approximating the quantum value of tilted XOR games to constant precision is RE-complete. Also, our result extends to succinct versions of tilted XOR games, where the questions can be polynomial-length binary strings, generated by a polynomial-time verifier.   For classical strategies, the distinction between XOR games and tilted XOR games is inconsequential. Håstad (J. ACM, 2001) shows that they are both NP-complete to approximate, by using a reduction from linear systems to XOR games. Our approach is to show that this is also quantum-sound, but as a reduction from linear system games to tilted XOR games.   Since titled XOR games are a special case of binary games (where each party outputs a single bit), our result implies that binary games are RE-hard to approximate.
summary: This paper analyzes the difficulty of approximating the quantum value for a specific class of nonlocal games called tilted XOR games. By reducing known hard computational problems like E3-LIN and the halting problem to these games, the authors prove that approximation is RE-complete. This result establishes a deep link between quantum information theory and high levels of computational complexity.
main_problem: The core problem is determining the computational complexity of approximating the quantum value for a generalized class of nonlocal games called 'tilted XOR games.'
main_result: The authors prove that approximating the quantum value of tilted XOR games to constant precision is RE-complete, implying that general binary nonlocal games are hard to approximate.
method: The hardness result is established via a polynomial-time reduction from E3-LIN games (linear constraint systems) and later extended using reductions involving the halting problem for tracial strategies.
model_or_system: The study focuses on quantum nonlocal games, specifically 'tilted XOR games,' which are binary games whose winning condition is a slight variation of simple XOR constraints. The analysis extends to quantum tracial strategies ($\omega^*_{tr}(G)$).
key_observables: The primary observable is the quantum value (or approximation thereof) of the game, $\omega^*(G)$ or $\omega^*_{tr}(G)$.
important_parameters: The complexity depends on parameters like completeness probability ($c$) and soundness probability ($s$), which define the decision problem thresholds.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on reductions from known hard problems (E3-LIN, halting problem) and utilizes characterizations of optimal strategies for XOR games.
figures_summary: Figure 1 summarizes complexity regions for classical and quantum values ($	ext{TXOR}_{c,s}$ vs $	ext{TXOR}^*_{c,s}$), highlighting a red triangular region labeled RE indicating the hardness boundary.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the general RE-completeness result for tilted XOR games. It then refines this analysis using specific parameters ($c, s$) and extends the hardness proof to quantum tracial strategies ($\omega^*_{tr}(G)$) via a reduction from the halting problem.
why_interesting: This work connects fundamental concepts in computational complexity theory (RE-completeness) directly to the physical limitations of quantum correlations, providing theoretical boundaries on what can be efficiently verified or simulated using quantum resources.
